speaker: Jonathan Gray
title: Blackstone's Jon Gray on real estate, rates, and building a winning company culture
question: In developed markets, why has power and energy infrastructure shifted from a sleepy utility sector into a major growth area?
guest: People think of power and energy as not that exciting. Today it actually is because two mega trends are happening at the same time. One, many companies and countries are trying to move from hydrocarbons, particularly coal, to renewables, so that's impacting where the supply of power is coming from in a very big way. And then on the demand side, after twenty years of flat power demand in most developed markets, because of electrification of cars, because of some reshoring, and particularly because of data centers, we're seeing this huge surge of demand. So what does that mean? Well, build lots of renewables. Invest in transmission to the extent you can. It also means traditional hydrocarbons—that's an important part of this. And then there are all sorts of services that utilities need, software consultancy, grid hardening, as this electrification wave continues.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core reason is that electricity demand in developed markets is growing again after roughly two decades of being flat. From the mid-2000s, efficiency gains and the offshoring of heavy industry offset economic growth, so utilities were slow, dividend-style businesses with little need for new capacity.

Several forces have ended that at once. AI and cloud data centres are the most visible, with single campuses now requesting as much power as a mid-sized city. Electrification of transport, heating and industrial processes adds further load, as does the reshoring of manufacturing such as semiconductor and battery plants.

At the same time, the supply side needs heavy investment. Much of the grid is decades old and due for replacement, the shift to renewables requires new transmission, storage and backup capacity, and energy security has become a political priority since the 2022 energy crisis.

The result is a large, multi-year capital spending cycle meeting constrained supply: long interconnection queues, and shortages of transformers, turbines and skilled labour. That gives pricing power and earnings growth to utilities, equipment makers and independent power producers, supported by government subsidies and regulated returns on an expanding asset base.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
For decades, electricity demand in developed markets was essentially flat as energy-efficiency gains and industrial offshoring offset economic growth, leaving utilities as slow-growing, dividend-focused businesses. That stagnation has reversed into a structural surge in power consumption driven simultaneously by hyperscale AI data centers, the electrification of transport and heating, and the reshoring of energy-intensive manufacturing such as semiconductors and batteries.

Meeting this sudden load growth requires a massive capital-spending cycle across the entire energy system. Infrastructure owners must urgently expand and modernize aging transmission and distribution grids, replace retiring coal and older gas plants, and integrate vast amounts of intermittent wind and solar alongside battery storage, natural gas, and nuclear generation to ensure round-the-clock reliability. Because grid interconnection and fast access to firm power have become critical economic bottlenecks—reinforced by government industrial policies and energy-security priorities—utilities, independent power producers, and grid-equipment makers now command stronger pricing power, lucrative long-term contracts with creditworthy tech buyers, and decades of visible rate-base and earnings growth.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: For roughly 15 to 20 years, electricity demand in the US and Europe was basically flat. Efficiency gains offset economic growth, and the heavy-industry base shrank. So utilities were treated as low-growth bond substitutes. That has reversed, mainly because of several demand drivers arriving at once. The biggest is AI and data centers, whose power needs are growing very fast and now dominate utility load forecasts. Electrification adds more: electric vehicles, heat pumps, and industrial processes switching from fossil fuels to electricity. Onshoring of manufacturing, especially semiconductors and batteries backed by subsidies such as the US Inflation Reduction Act and CHIPS Act, brings large new industrial loads. On the supply side, aging grids and power plants need replacing. The energy transition also requires huge investment in renewables, storage, transmission and grid modernization, and gas and nuclear are getting new attention for firm, around-the-clock power. Grid connection queues and equipment shortages, such as transformers, turbines and switchgear, give pricing power to suppliers and rate-base growth to regulated utilities. Together, these have turned power infrastructure into one of the clearest ways to invest in AI and decarbonization.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
For decades, electricity demand in developed markets remained largely flat thanks to efficiency gains and offshoring, leaving power and energy infrastructure as a slow-growth, defensive sector. That dynamic has reversed sharply due to a convergence of structural demand drivers. Most prominently, the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud computing has triggered an unprecedented buildout of power-hungry data centers. At the same time, the broad electrification of transportation, heating, and industrial processes—combined with the reshoring of domestic manufacturing—is steadily adding new load to the grid.

Meeting this surge while transitioning toward cleaner and more secure energy sources requires massive capital investment. Integrating intermittent wind and solar power, deploying battery storage, and replacing aging transmission and distribution networks demand trillions of dollars in grid modernization and new generation capacity, including nuclear and natural gas backup. Because utilities and infrastructure operators earn regulated or long-term contracted returns on deployed capital, this historic investment cycle has transformed a once-sleepy sector into a major growth engine.

Electricity demand is growing again after years of little growth in many developed markets. AI and cloud data centers need large amounts of reliable power, while electric vehicles, heat pumps, and some industrial processes are shifting energy use from fossil fuels to electricity. New manufacturing plants are adding demand in some regions.

At the same time, utilities need to replace aging equipment and build grids that can connect renewable generation and deliver power where demand is rising. That means investment in transmission lines, substations, storage, and generation that can supply power when wind and solar output is low. Energy security and resilience to extreme weather add to the need for upgrades. The sector has become a growth area because it has to expand capacity and modernize the system at the same time, creating years of investment across utilities, equipment suppliers, and developers.
